labels.answer: Colonization: start to form protective matrix

cloze.text: Microbiology is the study of algae, {{c1::bacteria}}, {{c2::fungi}}, {{c3::prions}}, protists, protozoa, and {{c4::viruses}}.
Bacteria are the {{c1::simplest}} creatures that are considered to be alive.
Bacteria lack a {{c1::membrane-bound nucleus}} and other internal structures, so they are ranked among the unicellular life forms called {{c2::prokaryotes}}.
A {{c1::virus}} is a small microorganism that requires a {{c2::host::what?}} (animals, plants, or bacteria) into which it injects its {{c3::RNA or DNA}} to reproduce.
Viruses are not plants, animals, or prokaryotic bacteria; they are placed in {{c1::their own kingdom}}.
Fungi (mold, mushrooms, yeasts) are {{c1::eukaryotic}} organisms: they contain {{c2::membrane-bound organelles}} and clearly defined nuclei.
Fungi are everywhere (soil, air, human body) and reproduce by forming vast quantities of {{c1::spores}}.
Bacteria are present in {{c1::all}} parts of the body, including every part of the mouth (cheek, palate, lips, tongue, teeth, gingiva, bone).
The {{c1::morphology (shape)}} of bacteria is a fundamental characteristic used for their classification and identification.
Diplococci are {{c1::pairs}} of cocci; streptococci are {{c2::chains}} of cocci; staphylococci are {{c3::clusters}} of cocci.
cloze.extra: Same prefixes for bacilli: diplobacilli = pairs, streptobacilli = chains.

cloze.text: {{c1::Tetrads}} are clusters of four cocci in a square arrangement.
A {{c1::coccobacillus}} is an oval or short, plump rod: a mix between a coccus and a bacillus.
Spirochetes are highly motile thanks to specialized internal flagella called {{c1::endoflagella}}, which let them corkscrew through viscous environments.
Spirochetes are often associated with {{c1::periodontal disease}}.
Compared with supragingival bacteria, subgingival bacteria are more {{c1::anaerobic}} and more {{c2::motile}}.
Of the oxygen groups, {{c1::aerobic}} bacteria are described as less harmful.
In the gram-negative cell envelope, the thin {{c1::peptidoglycan}} layer lies in the {{c2::periplasmic space}} between the outer membrane and the cytoplasmic membrane.
The outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria carries {{c1::lipopolysaccharides}} on its surface and is crossed by channel proteins called {{c2::porins}}.
The gram stain classifies bacteria by their {{c1::cell wall}} characteristics.
In the gram stain, gram-positive bacteria stain {{c1::purple}} with crystal violet; gram-negative bacteria stain {{c2::red (or pink)}} with the counterstain.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: the "P" in Positive = Purple; think Red = Negative.

cloze.text: Gram-positive bacteria have a {{c1::thick}}, single peptidoglycan layer that {{c2::retains}} the crystal violet stain.
Gram-negative bacteria have a {{c1::thin}} peptidoglycan layer that does not retain crystal violet, so the {{c2::red counterstain}} is visible.
Gram-positive bacteria have a {{c1::single}} cell wall, where the thick peptidoglycan surrounds the inner cell membrane.
Gram-negative bacteria have a {{c1::double}} cell wall: the thin peptidoglycan is sandwiched between an {{c2::inner and an outer}} cell membrane.
cloze.extra: Think of it as two "layers of walls".

cloze.text: Gram-positive bacteria primarily release {{c1::exotoxins}}; gram-negative bacteria can release {{c2::both exotoxins and endotoxins}}.
In the oral cavity, {{c1::gram-negative}} bacteria are considered more harmful or virulent, largely because they release potent {{c2::endotoxins}} upon cell death.
cloze.extra: Gram-positive bacteria are generally considered less harmful in oral infections.

cloze.text: The suffix {{c1::-toxin}} means poison: a poisonous or harmful substance, often produced by bacteria.
The prefix {{c1::exo-}} means outside / out of; the prefix {{c2::endo-}} means within / internal.
Compared with exotoxins, endotoxins are much {{c1::more}} heat-stable.
The root {{c1::-aero-}} means air/oxygen; the prefix {{c2::an-}} means not/without.
Facultative means {{c1::capable of / having the ability to do something optional}}, so facultative anaerobes can live with or without oxygen.
Oral bacteria that live in {{c1::supragingival}} plaque tend to be aerobic; those in deep periodontal pockets and the {{c2::subgingival}} biofilm tend to be anaerobic.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: HIV (causes AIDS) is transmitted mainly through {{c1::blood and blood products}}, including blood present in the oral cavity.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Hepatitis B virus is transmitted through {{c1::blood, saliva, and all other body fluids}}; the {{c2::hepatitis B vaccine}} is recommended for dental professionals.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Hepatitis C virus is transmitted mainly by {{c1::percutaneous}} (through-the-skin) exposure to blood, which makes {{c2::needlestick prevention}} crucial in dentistry.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1, HSV-2) causes herpetic {{c1::gingivostomatitis}}, herpes labialis (cold sores), ocular herpes, herpetic {{c2::whitlow}}, and genital herpes.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: HSV spreads by saliva, {{c1::direct}} contact (lip, hand, lesion), and {{c2::indirect}} contact (contaminated instruments, dental unit surfaces).

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes certain {{c1::oropharyngeal cancers}} and warts; it is transmitted by {{c2::sexual contact}}, including oral-genital contact.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Varicella-zoster virus causes {{c1::chickenpox}} (varicella) and {{c2::shingles}} (zoster); it spreads by direct contact, indirect contact with vesicular fluid, and airborne droplets.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Epstein-Barr virus causes infectious {{c1::mononucleosis}} and oral {{c2::hairy leukoplakia}}; it spreads by direct contact with oral secretions, mainly saliva ("kissing disease").

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Mumps virus is spread by {{c1::saliva}} and airborne droplets.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Poliovirus (poliomyelitis) spreads by saliva and respiratory droplets, and also by the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Influenza viruses spread through {{c1::nasal discharge}} and respiratory droplets.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Rubeola is the common name for {{c1::measles}}; rubella is {{c2::German measles}}.
cloze.extra: Measles: saliva, airborne droplets, direct contact with respiratory secretions. Rubella: nasopharyngeal secretions, direct contact, airborne droplets.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) is transmitted by airborne {{c1::droplet nuclei}} from coughing/sneezing, sputum, and saliva.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: {{c1::Treponema pallidum}} causes syphilis, spread by direct contact with infectious lesions (e.g., {{c2::chancre}}, mucous patch), often sexually but can involve oral lesions.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: {{c1::Bordetella pertussis}} causes whooping cough, spread by direct contact with respiratory discharges.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) causes {{c1::scarlet fever}}, impetigo, and {{c2::strep throat}}.
cloze.extra: Spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact with nose/throat secretions or skin lesions.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Streptococcus {{c1::pneumoniae}} causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis; it spreads by respiratory droplets and contact with respiratory secretions.

cloze.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
cloze.text: Candida albicans causes candidiasis (oral thrush), usually as an {{c1::opportunistic}} infection (overgrowth of normal flora) rather than person-to-person spread.
In the biofilm lifecycle, free-floating bacteria are in the {{c1::planktonic}} phase; attached, organized communities are in the {{c2::biofilm}} phase.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Dental plaque (dental biofilm) is a dense, {{c1::non-mineralized}}, organized community of bacterial colonies.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: In dental plaque, microorganisms are encased in a protective gel-like "{{c1::slime layer}}" (extracellular matrix) that contains fluid channels for {{c2::nutrient/waste}} exchange.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Calculus forms by precipitation of {{c1::calcium and phosphate}} salts from {{c2::saliva}} into the plaque matrix.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Dental plaque consists of {{c1::live}}, organized bacterial colonies, often appears yellowish or whitish, and is detected with {{c2::disclosing solutions}}.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Plaque {{c1::cannot}} be removed by rinsing or normal water flow.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: The mushroom-shaped plaque colonies have a {{c1::narrow}} base attached to the surface.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Calculus is a hard, calcified deposit that can be yellowish, brown, or black and is always covered by a layer of {{c1::dental plaque}}.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: The {{c1::porous}} nature of calculus provides a reservoir for bacteria and endotoxins.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Plaque adheres to moist oral surfaces, including teeth, existing {{c1::calculus}}, and dental restorations.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Plaque requires {{c1::physical/mechanical disruption}} for removal (toothbrushing, flossing, instrumentation if subgingival).

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Calculus attaches to teeth, dental restorations, implants, and dental appliances; it {{c1::cannot}} be removed by brushing or flossing and requires professional {{c2::scaling (debridement)}} with specialized instruments.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Calculus worsens plaque accumulation because of its {{c1::rough}} surface.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Materia alba loosely adheres to tooth surfaces and soft tissues and can typically be removed by {{c1::rinsing or a water spray}} or routine toothbrushing.

cloze.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
cloze.text: Materia alba is generally {{c1::less}} adherent than plaque; its presence indicates {{c2::poor oral hygiene}} and can contribute to gingival inflammation.

Plaque formation step 1: a thin coating of {{c1::salivary proteins}} called the pellicle attaches to the tooth surface (including restorations and calculus) within {{c2::minutes}} after a professional cleaning.
The pellicle {{c1::protects}} the enamel from acidic activity.
The pellicle's {{c1::double-sided adhesive}} property facilitates attachment of bacteria to the tooth surface.
The pellicle is {{c1::not visible}} with disclosing agent, but it can become stained with time.
Step 2: {{c1::planktonic}} (free-floating) bacteria attach to the outer surface of the pellicle with hair-like structures called {{c2::fimbriae}} and form microcolonies.
A bacterial colony is composed of {{c1::many}} different kinds of bacteria.
Step 3: bacterial microcolonies form a sessile mushroom shape, {{c1::narrow}} at the base and {{c2::wide}} at the top.
Microcolonies grow primarily through {{c1::cell division}} rather than through the attachment of new bacteria.
A {{c1::slime layer}} protects the bacterial community and helps the biofilm grow.
Step 4 (maturation): the bacterial composition changes to a more {{c1::toxic}} mix, and the biofilm extends into the {{c2::subgingival}} region to form mature biofilm.
After a few {{c1::days}} of undisturbed plaque formation, the gingival margin becomes inflamed.
cloze.extra: Compare the clinical tip on p.320: inflammation starts after about a week (7-14 days).

cloze.text: Within the first 2 days of plaque formation, {{c1::gram-positive cocci}} are prevalent.
After 2-4 days, gram-positive cocci increase in number and {{c1::gram-positive rods}} appear.
After 4-7 days, gram-negative {{c1::spirochetes}} (spiral) and {{c2::vibrios}} (comma-shaped) appear.
After 14-21 days, {{c1::gram-negative/anaerobic}} bacteria are prevalent and {{c2::gingivitis}} is visible.
Dental biofilm and bacteria are the {{c1::primary factors}} in the initiation and progression of caries and periodontal diseases.
Bacteria are {{c1::transmissible}}; therefore caries and periodontal diseases are transmissible.
Biofilm accumulates most on the {{c1::gingival margin}}.
The {{c1::palatal}} surfaces of the maxillary teeth accumulate the least biofilm because the {{c2::tongue}} naturally cleans them.
Teeth {{c1::crowding}}, uneven surfaces, or pits contribute to plaque accumulation and make removal more difficult.
{{c1::Mechanical}} removal is the only effective way to remove plaque.
Carious lesions can be {{c1::cavitated}} (with a hole) or {{c2::non-cavitated}} (without a hole).
A non-cavitated carious lesion can be different in color and is usually {{c1::whiter}}.
In demineralization, the minerals {{c1::calcium and phosphorus}} are removed from tooth structure by {{c2::acid}}.
White lesions are {{c1::subsurface}} demineralization under the outer layer of the tooth and are {{c2::smooth}} in texture.
Do {{c1::not}} use ultrasonic or sharp instruments on demineralized areas; use {{c2::blunt}} instruments and avoid scratching them.
Arrested caries are areas where demineralization has {{c1::stopped}}; they are usually {{c2::darker}} in color than the original structure.
Radiographically, caries appear {{c1::radiolucent}}.
For visual caries detection, {{c1::dry}} the tooth and use {{c2::light}} to detect darker areas.
Carious lesions at the beginning are {{c1::white}}.
The 3 components needed for caries formation are {{c1::fermentable carbohydrates}}, {{c2::bacteria}}, and {{c3::tooth structure}}.
Mutans streptococci are gram-positive, {{c1::non-motile}} cocci.
Streptococcus {{c1::mutans}} is mainly responsible for caries formation; Streptococcus {{c2::sobrinus}} is often associated with {{c3::smooth surface}} caries.
Lactobacillus (gram-positive {{c1::rods}}) plays a role in caries {{c2::progression}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: L in Lactobacillus = L in Late: lactobacilli act in the late stage of caries.

cloze.text: {{c1::Actinomyces}} species (e.g., A. naeslundii) are associated with {{c2::root}} caries.
{{c1::Bifidobacteria}} are associated with {{c2::childhood}} caries.
Mutans streptococci and bifidobacteria are most active in the {{c1::initial}} stage of caries formation.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: S in Streptococcus = S in Start: streptococcus "starts" the caries process.

basic.back: Bacteria that cannot survive in the presence of oxygen (oxygen is toxic to them)
basic.extra: They flourish in oxygen-deprived places such as deep periodontal pockets and the subgingival biofilm.

basic.back: Bacteria that can survive and grow with or without oxygen

basic.front: Why is the gram-stain result clinically useful?
basic.back: It often correlates with the bacterium's pathogenicity and its susceptibility to antimicrobial agents.
A harmful substance produced inside bacteria and released (excreted, "exported") into the surroundings while the bacteria live and grow
A toxin that is a component of the bacterial cell wall itself (gram-negative bacteria), released only when the cell dies and breaks apart (lysis)
basic.extra: Much more heat-stable than exotoxins. WakeUpMemory: ENDOtoxins are ENDured until the bacteria ENDs its life.

basic.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
basic.front: Biofilm vs. dental plaque: what is the difference?
basic.back: A biofilm is any group of microbes sticking to a wet surface (pipes, medical tools, etc.); dental plaque is a type of biofilm that forms on teeth and other surfaces in the mouth. All plaque is biofilm, but not all biofilm is plaque.

basic.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
basic.back: Mineralized dental plaque

basic.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
basic.back: Soft, sticky, white deposit of bacteria, food debris, desquamated epithelial cells, and other organic/inorganic material
basic.extra: Resembles "cottage cheese"; lacks the organized structure of dental plaque.

basic.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
basic.front: Why is mechanical removal of plaque paramount?
basic.back: The slime layer protects the bacteria from antibiotics, antimicrobials, and the host immune system.
A hole caused by demineralization of the tooth structure
The process of cavity formation
The initial occurrence of decay on a tooth surface that has never been restored

mcq.question: Which statement about fungi is correct?
options: A. They are prokaryotes that reproduce by binary fission
B. They are eukaryotes that reproduce by forming spores
C. They must inject RNA or DNA into a host cell to reproduce
mcq.answer: B. They are eukaryotes that reproduce by forming spores
mcq.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotic (membrane-bound organelles, defined nuclei) and reproduce by forming vast quantities of spores. Binary fission and the lack of membrane-bound organelles describe bacteria (prokaryotes); injecting nucleic acid into a host describes viruses.

mcq.question: A smear of subgingival plaque from a deep periodontal pocket shows very thin, flexible, highly motile spiral organisms. These are most likely
mcq.explanation: Spirochetes are very thin, elongated, flexible spirals that move by endoflagella and are often associated with periodontal disease. Coccobacilli are short plump rods; staphylococci and streptobacilli are clusters of cocci and chains of rods.

mcq.question: Which feature explains why a bacterium appears red/pink after gram staining?
options: A. A thick peptidoglycan layer that retains crystal violet
B. A thin peptidoglycan layer that does not retain crystal violet
C. Absence of a cell wall
D. A single cell membrane surrounded by thick peptidoglycan
mcq.answer: B. A thin peptidoglycan layer that does not retain crystal violet
mcq.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer between two membranes; it loses the crystal violet, so the red counterstain shows. A thick, single peptidoglycan layer is the gram-positive (purple) structure.

mcq.question: Gram-negative bacteria are generally considered more virulent in the oral cavity than gram-positive bacteria mainly because they
options: A. Stain purple with crystal violet
B. Have a thick peptidoglycan wall
C. Release potent endotoxins when the cell dies
mcq.answer: C. Release potent endotoxins when the cell dies
mcq.explanation: Endotoxins are part of the gram-negative cell wall and are released on lysis; they are highly heat-stable. Purple staining and a thick peptidoglycan wall describe gram-positive bacteria.

mcq.question: Which is TRUE of endotoxins?
options: A. They are actively secreted while bacteria grow
B. They are produced mainly by gram-positive bacteria
C. They are released when the cell wall breaks apart (lysis)
D. They are less heat-stable than exotoxins
mcq.answer: C. They are released when the cell wall breaks apart (lysis)
mcq.explanation: Endotoxins are components of the gram-negative cell wall, released only on lysis, and are highly heat-stable. Active secretion during growth describes exotoxins, which are the main toxins of gram-positive bacteria and are less heat-stable.

mcq.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
mcq.question: A dental hygienist develops a painful vesicular infection of the finger after treating a patient with active cold sores without gloves. The causative organism is most likely
mcq.explanation: Herpetic whitlow is an HSV infection of the finger, spread by direct contact with lesions or saliva. Varicella-zoster causes chickenpox and shingles; EBV causes mononucleosis and oral hairy leukoplakia.

mcq.section: Pathogens transmissible from the oral cavity
mcq.question: For which pathogen is the vaccine specifically recommended for dental professionals because it spreads through blood, saliva and all other body fluids?
mcq.explanation: HBV is transmitted by blood, saliva and all body fluids, and the hepatitis B vaccine is recommended for dental professionals. HCV spreads mainly by percutaneous blood exposure and has no vaccine listed; prevention relies on avoiding needlesticks.

mcq.section: Common deposits in the oral cavity
mcq.question: A patient presents with a soft, white, cottage-cheese-like deposit along the gingival margin that comes off with a forceful air-water spray. This deposit is most likely
mcq.explanation: Materia alba is a loosely adherent, unorganized deposit (bacteria, food debris, desquamated cells) that can be rinsed away. Plaque is organized and cannot be removed by rinsing or water flow; calculus requires scaling.

mcq.question: Which structure allows planktonic bacteria to attach to the acquired pellicle?
mcq.explanation: Planktonic bacteria attach to the outer surface of the pellicle with hair-like fimbriae, then form microcolonies. Flagella and endoflagella are for motility.

mcq.question: A patient has not cleaned his teeth for 3 weeks and has visible gingivitis. Which bacteria predominate in his plaque?
options: D. Aerobic gram-positive cocci and rods equally
mcq.explanation: By 14-21 days gram-negative/anaerobic bacteria are prevalent and gingivitis is visible. Gram-positive cocci dominate the first 2 days; gram-positive rods appear at 2-4 days.

mcq.question: During an exam, the hygienist sees a chalky white, smooth, non-cavitated area on a dried facial surface. What is the best action?
options: A. Probe it firmly with a sharp explorer to test for softness
B. Remove the stain with the ultrasonic scaler
C. Examine it visually and with a blunt instrument, avoiding scratching
D. Record it as arrested caries
mcq.answer: C. Examine it visually and with a blunt instrument, avoiding scratching
mcq.explanation: A white, smooth lesion is subsurface demineralization (an early, non-cavitated lesion). Sharp or ultrasonic instruments must not be used on demineralized areas. Arrested caries are usually darker, not white.

mcq.question: An older patient with gingival recession has new carious lesions on exposed root surfaces. Which bacteria are most associated with this type of caries?
mcq.explanation: Actinomyces species (e.g., A. naeslundii) are associated with root caries. S. sobrinus is linked to smooth surface caries, bifidobacteria to childhood caries, and lactobacilli to caries progression.
